quote: Well, we we had someone come and visit us, you know, just kinda going door to door talking about solar and said, oh, man. Maybe this is something to look into.
stewart_read: Customer discloses a door-to-door solar encounter that sparked his interest, but the rep never asks which company or what was pitched.
alternative_hypothesis: Rep may have judged this detail as irrelevant since the customer moved on to discussing a prior Ion/PPA experience, making further probing low-value.
coaching_implication: A 10-second follow-up ('who was that with?') would have surfaced competitive intel worth passing to the closer.

quote: we we looked a few years back about the with Ionic about buying, and that just wasn't the right fit for us.
stewart_read: Customer reveals a prior Ion (or similarly-named company) purchase quote that didn't fit, and separately mentions comparing lease/PPA options — real competitive and structural context that the rep lets pass without asking why it didn't fit or what changed.
alternative_hypothesis: The rep may have implicitly filed this as 'now considering lease/PPA instead of purchase' and let the specialist unpack it, which is defensible scope discipline.
coaching_implication: Even a single clarifying question ('what wasn't the right fit last time?') gives the closer a huge head start avoiding the same rejection reason.

quote: I guess if your wife isn't on the title, then we could just do it with you.
stewart_read: The customer never confirmed whether his wife is on the title — he said 'maybe my wife... I'd have to look at that' — and the rep used that unresolved uncertainty to default to excluding her from the appointment. protocols.spouse_decision is explicit that co-decision-makers should be included in the appointment; the rep should have asked the customer to confirm rather than guessing off an ambiguous answer.
alternative_hypothesis: None credible — the schema's correct_response_pattern is unambiguous (include the spouse), and the rep had already, minutes earlier, told the customer the specialist would meet 'with you and your wife,' making this a self-contradicted protocol miss rather than a defensible judgment call.
coaching_implication: Coach the rep to explicitly resolve title/co-owner status before booking, and to default to including the spouse when ownership is unclear rather than defaulting to exclusion — this appointment is now structurally vulnerable if the wife is in fact a co-owner and the closer needs both there to close.

quote: No problem. So, yeah, I can try I can give you some information. I don't know, like, as much as a specialist, of course, just because I'm a scheduler. But Yeah. We have a pretty good program right now, I'd say. So what it does is it guarantees you savings within the first year you have solar.
stewart_read: Rep verbally flags the scope boundary ('just because I'm a scheduler') and then immediately crosses it by describing the savings-guarantee program's mechanics.
alternative_hypothesis: This could be read as a light legitimacy-building move rather than true scope creep since it's brief and doesn't get into technical specs or pricing.
coaching_implication: Praise the instinct to name the boundary, but redirect the content itself — the universal escape hatch line would have kept this cleaner and preserved specialist value.

quote: it's up to $2.70 in the summer and down to, you know, $1.01 $1.50 in the winter.
stewart_read: Customer hands over a real bill range (seasonally variable, $150-$270), a strong anchor point, but the rep only acknowledges it generically before moving to the mechanical bill-document ask.
alternative_hypothesis: The rep did tie the bill lightly to ComEd's rate increases at 03:25, which is a partial flip rather than a total miss.
coaching_implication: Encourage the rep to reflect the specific number back as the customer's own reason to act ('so you're looking at potentially cutting that $270 summer bill') rather than a general statement about the utility raising rates.

quote: We can definitely help get that cut down. I know that ComEd is they've been raising their rates quite a bit from what I've heard, so I'm glad you guys are looking into an an alternative.
stewart_read: This is the rep's flip attempt — turning the bill number into a reason to act by pointing at rising ComEd rates — but it's generalized ('from what I've heard') rather than tied directly to the customer's own $150-$270 figure.
alternative_hypothesis: This could be read as a full flip since it does connect the bill pain to urgency; the softness is in delivery, not strategy.
coaching_implication: Coach the rep to make this flip more specific and confident — replace 'from what I've heard' with a direct callback to the customer's own number.

quote: Yeah. I'm trying to pull up my calendar, but for some reason, my password isn't working.
stewart_read: Rep admits a live technical problem transparently rather than stalling or fabricating availability, then recovers by working from memory.
coaching_implication: This is a positive transparency model worth reinforcing — admit-and-recover beat other options here.
